summaries.summary: Public debates juxtapose diverging viewpoints and allow interactive attacks and defenses, making the resulting flow of ideas a key conversational feature.
This work introduces a computational framework characterizing debates by conversational flow, tracking promoting one's own points and attacking opponents' points to predict persuasion.
Oxford-style debates provide a convenient setting because two teams persuade a live audience whose votes before and after isolate conversational flow effects.
Opening statements present arguments before discussion, allowing identification of prior talking points separately from points introduced spontaneously during interaction.
This work introduces a debate dataset with rich metadata, proposes a framework for tracking idea flow, and shows effectiveness in a predictive setting.
The study uses IQ2 Oxford-style debate transcripts and results, with two opposing teams, a moderator, three rounds, 7-minute introductions, 30-minute discussions, and 2-minute conclusions.
The dataset contains transcripts of all IQ2 US debates from September 2006 to September 2015, totaling 108 debates averaging 12801 words in 117 turns.
Winning side labels follow IQ2's delta criterion, and for 30% of debates the winning and losing sides' deltas differ by less than 10%.
Audience feedback checks show winning teams receive more laughter during discussion and more applause during conclusion, while introduction reactions are similar.
The running example is the “Millennials don't stand a chance” debate, where the For side won with a delta of 20% versus 5% for Against.
The methodology identifies promoting one's own points and addressing the opponent's points, then investigates their usage and effect on debate outcome.
Talking points are identified using monroe2008fightin's log-odds ratio with a uniform Dirichlet prior on introduction word usage, selecting words with highest and lowest z-scores.
Self-coverage and opponent-coverage quantify strategies as fractions of content words in a round covering a side's own or opposing talking points.
Self-coverage dominates discussion, but interaction causes a sharp drop in self-coverage and a rise in opponent-coverage when discussion begins.
Winning sides show slightly larger drops in self-coverage and in summed self- and opponent-coverage, suggesting they steer away from either side's talking points.
Discussion points are words introduced during discussion and adopted by opponents at least twice; only 3% qualify, about 10 discussion points per debate.
Eventual winners adopt more opponent-introduced discussion points than losers, raising topic control and contesting interpretations of strategic advantage.
Post-hoc examination finds 78% of valid discussion points are picked up to be challenged, supporting that winners engage with opponents' ideas.
Predictive power is evaluated by binary classification of whether For or Against wins, aiming to understand which developed flow features carry predictive power.
Flow features include self-coverage, opponent-coverage, their sum, the drop in self-coverage, and the number of discussion points adopted by each side.
Baseline features use number of words uttered and number of turns taken as length, plus a unigram baseline (BOW).
Audience features use counts of applause and laughter received by each side as rough indicators of how well the audience foresees outcomes.
Prediction accuracy uses leave-one-out (LOO), logistic regression, 3-fold cross-validation, and univariate feature selection in the Flow* setting.
Flow features achieve the best accuracy (Flow: 63%; Flow*: 65%), above a 50% random baseline and comparable to audience features (60%), while length and BOW do not beat chance.
Flow* most often selects adopted discussion points, recall of talking points during discussion, and drop in own talking point usage, suggesting audiences favor discussion-emphasizing strategies.
Related work models dialogue acts, conversation-level traits, participant stances, and stance-characterizing words, while known debate stances and turn structure allow focusing on outcome.
Argumentation strategy research has focused on monologic arguments and forum challenges; this work complements it by studying relative persuasiveness in extended multi-turn conversations.
Prior influence studies in political conversations examined topic control, linguistic style matching, and turn-taking; this work explores idea flow in a highly structured setting.
Future work could use topic models or word embeddings, add linguistic choices, compare monologic and interactive dynamics, and clarify strategic implications of dialogue versus self-promotion.
Simplifying assumptions include a basic unigram-based definition of discussion points that ignores context and semantic sense, motivating improved retrieval models.
The Oxford-style debate dataset is limited in size, and future work could examine flow features in Wikipedia talk pages, education, and cooperative work.
The authors thank reviewers, V. Niculae, I. Arawjo, and D. Sedra, and acknowledge support in part by a Google Faculty Research Award.
